scenes.name: Alicia, la locura y el regreso a la infancia
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Al final de 1966 el LSD llevó al pop de vuelta a la infancia y a la locura. Los Beatles empezaron el 24 de noviembre «Strawberry Fields Forever», un viaje de Lennon hacia abajo, no hacia atrás, al orfanato junto a su casa, «psicoanálisis con música», unida por Geoff Emerick a partir de dos tomas; luego «When I’m Sixty-Four» y «Penny Lane». En Navidad la BBC aplazó el Alice in Wonderland de Jonathan Miller, sin cabezas de animal, con el sitar de Ravi Shankar y rodado en un hospital militar de víctimas de neurosis de guerra: un catálogo de psicosis. Grace Slick llevó «White Rabbit» a Jefferson Airplane; Syd Barrett escribía sobre el mundo de Lewis Carroll. Proliferaban los discos sobre la locura («They’re Coming to Take Me Away, Ha-Haaa!», «Pandora’s Golden Heebie Jeebies» de los Association), y en el corazón secreto del año, la tristeza frágil de «How Can We Hang On to a Dream» de Tim Hardin.

podcast.title: Resignation from EMI (1965)
podcast.body: In 1965, George Martin resigned from EMI after the label repeatedly refused to modify his pay structure to include royalties. "And when EMI turned them down again to have his pay structure modified, he quit. That was 1965."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Beatles Collaboration with McCartney (1973)
podcast.body: George Martin, who built and ran Air Studios in London, agreed to produce the recording sessions for Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. This marked a significant reunion, as it was the first time Martin had worked with a Beatle since the conclusion of the "Abbey Road" sessions in 1969. Martin later compelled the Bond producers to use McCartney's version as the title sequence. "Martin agreed to produce the sessions marking this as the first time since the end of the Abbey Road sessions that he got to work with a beetle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Producer's Ultimatum for "Live and Let Die" (1973)
podcast.body: George Martin delivered an ultimatum to the Bond film producers regarding Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. He informed them that if they wanted the "very good theme song," they would have to use Paul's version for the title sequence, otherwise they would need to find someone else for their movie. Faced with time constraints, the producers, either Harry Saltzman or Albert Broccoli, conceded. "When it was done George Martin went to the producers and said look we've got a very good theme song for you but the only way you're going to get it is if you use Paul's version as the title sequence."

podcast.title: Producing America's Albums
podcast.body: While in Los Angeles to discuss the *Live and Let Die* score with Paul McCartney, George Martin agreed to meet with America. He subsequently produced their 1974 album *Holiday* and later served as both producer and conductor for the symphony orchestra on their 1975 live album, *America Live at the Hollywood Bowl*. "George Martin happened to be in LA to meet with Paul McCartney about the score for a live and let die and he agreed to meet with America and that was that he produced holiday which was released in 1974."

podcast.title: Salary Dispute with EMI
podcast.body: Despite The Beatles' immense success, George Martin, as an EMI employee, received only a "tiny weekly salary" and no royalties for his production work, which caused him considerable annoyance. "No matter how successful the Beatles became, no matter how many records they sold, George did not receive any royalties as their producer."

xref.title: Accidental Feedback Discovery
xref.body: On October 18, 1964, while at Abbey Road Studios, John Lennon accidentally discovered the controlled feedback sound used on "I Feel Fine." After Paul McCartney plucked a bass string, John leaned his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp and began to walk away, inadvertently causing the guitar to pick up the bass note and create feedback. Recognizing the unique sound, both Lennon and McCartney asked producer George Martin to capture it for their new song. "But then the guitar picked up the sound of that bass note and started feeding back, and the sound was really cool, but a total accident."

xref.title: Accidental Feedback Discovery
xref.body: On October 18, 1964, during a recording session at Abbey Road Studios, Paul McCartney accidentally initiated the controlled feedback sound that would be used on "I Feel Fine." He plucked a string on his bass, and when John Lennon laid his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp, the guitar picked up the bass note and started feeding back. Paul and John recognized the coolness of the sound and requested producer George Martin to record it. "The discovery began when Paul McCarty picked a string on his bass, Appropole of Nothing, and then John laid his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp and started to walk away."

xref.title: Defining Sound with Yamaha CP70BM
xref.body: Following their guitarist's departure, Tim Rice-Oxley acquired a Yamaha CP70BM, a hybrid acoustic electric grand piano, influenced by Beatles producer George Martin's preference for the instrument. Plugging it in produced a "massive sound" that instantly became the signature sound of Keane, distinguishing them by centering their music around the piano rather than the guitar, leading to alt rock hits. "as soon as we plugged it in, it made this massive sound, and we immediately knew it was the sound of Keene. It opened up everything for the band, which started having all rock hits like this."

xref.title: Goofy Song for Chris Martin's Child
xref.body: Coldplay formed the pseudonymous band The Nappys to record a goofy song and accompanying video called "I'm Your Baby's Daddy." This project was a personal endeavor by Chris Martin, dedicated to his then-wife Gwyneth Paltrow while she was expecting their first child, affectionately referred to as "Little Apple." Sir George Martin notably introduced the video in a curly red wig. "When she was expecting Little Apple, the band got together for a goofy song and video under the name The Nappy's."

xref.title: Signature Piano Sound with Yamaha CP70BM
xref.body: Tim Rice-Oxley acquired a Yamaha CP70BM, a hybrid acoustic electric grand piano, after learning that Beatles producer George Martin highly regarded it. Upon tracking down a used one and plugging it in, the instrument produced a "massive sound" that immediately became Keane's defining characteristic and opened up new musical possibilities, leading to alt rock hits. "He acquired a Yamaha CP70BM, a hybrid acoustic electric grand piano, after reading that the Beatles producer George Martin really liked this thing. He eventually tracked down a used one, and here's a quote, as soon as we plugged it in, it made this massive sound, and we immediately knew it was the sound of Keene."

"But the guy in the wig introducing the video is definitely Sir George Martin."
